newsitem.title: EGYPT: Palestinians-Israelis to resume Hebron talks.
newsitem.headline: Palestinians-Israelis to resume Hebron talks.

text.p: Palestinians and Israelis were set to resume formal talks on a Hebron deal on Wednesday that Israel said could be quickly resolved but that the PLO said were at an impasse.
Palestinian President Yasser Arafat, who paid a one-day visit to Egypt on Wednesday, was enraged by an Israeli redeployment plan presented on Tuesday night, describing it as a tragedy.
"It's a dangerous operation. It shows Israel's aggressive intentions in Hebron and shows complete and abhorrent racism," he told reporters in Cairo.
Arafat said the plan would among other things divide the West Bank town in two and give Israel the right to chase Arabs it wanted anywhere in Hebron including Palestinian-ruled areas.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said if there was no goodwill anything could be used to thwart the talks.

"We are conducting the negotiations with goodwill. We hope we will encounter the same attitude from the other side," Netanyahu told Israel's army radio. "If there is an attitude like that, I have no doubt that we can finish it, even quickly.
"If there is not an attitude like that then each thing can be used as an excuse why we haven't finished."
Palestinian negotiators and U.S. envoy Dennis Ross were in the Egptian Red Sea resort of Taba, awaiting the Israeli team.

"We urge the Israeli delegation to arrive in Taba...with a green light from Mr Netanyahu to engage seriously on a mechanism of implementation, so we can start showing progress by carrying out accords on the ground," Palestinian delegation head Saeb Erekat told Reuters.
Ross said the talks had a long way to go.
"There is a lot of differences and there is a lot to be done," he told reporters.

U.S.-sponsored talks on implementing the Hebron redeployment are in their second week. The decision to hold them was taken at a Washington summit after clashes last month in which 60 Palestinians and 15 Israelis were killed.
Israel insists it does not want to open the accord, but demands that security arrangements for 400 Jewish settlers living among more than 100,000 Palestinians be bolstered.
The Palestinians, backed by Israel's Arab neighbours, oppose any changes in the deal signed by Israel's previous government.
Arafat has been piling pressure on Israel to implement the Hebron redeployment, widely seen as a test of the new rightwing Israeli government's intentions towards peace.
Arafat also wants Israel to carry out other parts of the 1995 self-rule accord, including further redeployment from rural areas in the West Bank still under Israel control.
On Tuesday, he hosted Jordan's King Hussein, Israel's closest Arab ally, in self-ruled Jericho. The move was widely seen as an attempt to display Arab solidarity against Israel.
Jordanian Prime Minister Abdul-Karim al-Kabariti, also in Cairo, predicted a crisis if Israel failed to redeploy.
"I am hopeful but without the redeployment in Hebron I think that we will be having a crisis in hand," he said.
Egyptian Foreign Minister Amr Moussa was pessimistic.
"It is clear that the Palestinian side does not see any progress in the negotiations and that the position now does not bode well," he told reporters.
